title: The City of Labtayt

full_text:
In the ancient kingdom of Andalusia stood the royal city of Labtayt, which is Toledo. In the center of the city rose an ancient, mysterious palace whose gates had never been opened since the founding of the realm. Each king, upon ascending the throne, placed a new iron lock upon the massive bronze doors, until twenty-four locks gleamed upon the portals.

When the haughty King Roderic seized the crown, the venerable bishops and counselors brought him the twenty-fifth lock. But Roderic shook his head with arrogant disdain: 'Why should I add another lock like a frightened child? I am a monarch of valor! I shall break open these gates and discover what treasure my ancestors have locked away from my eyes.'

The elders fell upon their knees, pleading: 'Do not do this, sire! The ancient prophecy decrees that as long as the palace remains sealed, our kingdom shall flourish in peace, but if the locks are broken, strangers shall conquer our land.'

Deaf to their pleas, Roderic commanded his smiths to cut the twenty-four locks with iron chisels. The heavy bronze gates swung open with a groan of thunder, revealing a vast, dark hall paved with jasper and lined with statues of gold. In the center stood an ebony table bearing an ancient wooden coffer decorated with pearls.

Roderic seized the coffer, pried open the lid, and found within a scroll of parchment. When he unrolled the scroll, a painted fresco illuminated the hall: upon it were depicted Arabian horsemen armed with scimitars and lances, riding swift steeds across desert sands. Below the painting was written an ancient inscription:

'When these locks are broken and this coffer is unsealed, warriors wearing these turbans and bearing these lances shall cross the sea and conquer the kingdom of Andalusia.'

Roderic trembled, seized with sudden dread. He ordered the gates resealed, but it was too late. Within the year, the fleet of Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the straits, and Roderic’s army was scattered at the Guadalete, proving that he who scoffs at ancestral warnings invites his own destruction.
moral: Arrogance that tramples ancestral wisdom and breaks sacred locks unleashes unforeseen catastrophe.
